Self-inspection is a systematic internal review of whether pharmaceutical operations follow
Good Manufacturing Practice and the company quality system. It helps identify
weaknesses before they affect patients or product quality. A self-inspection program
should cover relevant people, premises, equipment, operations and records. The purpose
is to find and correct genuine problems, not simply to produce
a favorable score.
A useful self-inspection program defines scope, responsibilities, frequency and follow-up. Planning
can consider process criticality, past deviations, previous findings and changes. Inspectors
should be sufficiently knowledgeable and objective for the activity. Risk-based prioritization
helps allocate attention, but it does not justify omitting required GMP
controls. The plan should be documented under the site quality system.
Before an inspection, identify the approved procedures and records relevant to
the selected area. Examples may include training records, equipment logs, cleaning
records, deviations, change controls and qualification status. Inspectors should check the
current approved version and whether records reflect actual work. A tidy
folder alone does not demonstrate that an operation is controlled. Evidence
must be reliable and traceable.
During the inspection, observe work, interview personnel and compare actual practices
with approved requirements. Follow the process from material or personnel entry
through operations and recording. Ask neutral questions and document facts, not
assumptions. When a possible issue is found, capture enough objective evidence
to allow fair assessment. Escalate any immediate product quality or patient
safety concern through the site procedure.
Inspection findings should clearly describe the observed condition, applicable requirement or
procedure, and supporting evidence. The organization should assess the significance and
potential product impact of each finding. Classification terminology varies between quality
systems and authorities; do not assign a universal severity label without
an applicable framework. Reports should distinguish verified observations from recommendations and
should assign accountable follow-up.
Appropriate corrective action should address the causes of confirmed deficiencies, not
just the visible symptom. Action plans need responsible owners and justified
timelines. Some issues require investigation, product impact assessment, preventive measures or
training. Follow-up should verify implementation and, where appropriate, effectiveness. Closing a
finding solely because a document was signed does not prove that
the underlying problem is resolved.
Inspection readiness is sustained through routine GMP compliance, not a last-minute
cleanup before an audit. Current procedures, complete records, trained personnel and
equipment status controls help teams explain and demonstrate their processes. Management
review and trend analysis can reveal recurring weaknesses. Personnel should answer
accurately, acknowledge uncertainty and retrieve evidence through approved systems. Never fabricate
or backdate records to satisfy an inspector.
Consider an internal inspection of a sterile manufacturing support area. An
inspector notices that an equipment calibration label is expired while a
nearby logbook is incomplete. The team should secure the equipment as
required, verify the actual calibration and use status, and assess potential
impact on operations or product quality. The observation and decisions should
be documented and escalated. A new label alone is not an
adequate corrective action without confirming the underlying status.
